01.actor: Rabba bar bar Hanna (as eyewitness) and an Arab with his camel
01.event: Rabba bar bar Hanna reports that he saw an Arab cut open his camel with a sword, and it died before it even stopped braying.
01.turn: The camel died instantly, offered as proof that a cut-open animal cannot survive; Abaye replies the camel was emaciated.
01.outcome: Abaye dismisses the proof by saying that camel was weak.
01.summary: Rabba bar bar Hanna says he once saw an Arab slice open his camel with a sword, and the animal died before its braying even stopped. This is raised as evidence against Abaye's view that a cut-open creature might survive. Abaye answers that the camel was emaciated and so died at once.
01.missing: The anecdote is only a brief eyewitness proof inside a legal argument, with no further scene or aftermath.

02.actor: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak, Rabbi Zeira
02.event: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak danced before brides juggling three myrtle branches, unlike Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai who used one.
02.turn: Rabbi Zeira complained the old man was shaming the scholars, but when Shmuel died a pillar of fire separated him from everyone, a sign of rare greatness.
02.outcome: Rabbi Zeira reversed himself and said the branch (or nonsense, or method) had worked in the old man's favor.
02.summary: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai used to dance before brides with a myrtle branch, but Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggled three, and Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was embarrassing the scholars. When Shmuel died, a pillar of fire parted him from everyone else, a sign given to only one or two people per generation. Rabbi Zeira then said the old man's branch had done him good.

03.missing: The passage only reports that people of Judea were asked and said both spellings exist; this is a scholarly answer, not an event with a turn.

04.missing: It mentions an L-shaped alley in Neharde'a on which stringencies were imposed, but only as the occasion for a legal analysis of Rav's and Shmuel's rulings; no events happen.

05.actor: A resident of Eretz Yisrael and an Amorite (non-Jew)
05.event: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how many kor of dates he could pick from a palm on the Jordan bank, and he said sixty.
05.turn: The Amorite scoffed that the Israelites had ruined the land, since his people used to pick 120 kor from it.
05.outcome: The resident replied that he had only counted one side of the tree, topping the claim.
05.summary: An Amorite asked an Israelite how many kor of dates he gathered from a palm tree by the Jordan, and the Israelite said sixty. The Amorite said the Israelites had already ruined the land, for his people had picked 120 kor from it. The Israelite answered that he had only spoken of one side of the tree.

06.missing: The passage is a baraita dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages about re-circumcision, citing the days of ben Koziva only as legal evidence; no narrative.

07.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Elazar
07.event: While Rabbi Elazar and Reish Lakish sat before Rabbi Yohanan, a case of priestly status proved by first Torah reading came up, and Reish Lakish again asked whether the man was seen receiving teruma at the threshing floor.
07.turn: Rabbi Yohanan replied with the same retort Rabbi Elazar had earlier given, revealing that Rabbi Elazar had been quoting Yohanan.
07.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing the teaching in Yohanan's name.
07.summary: Earlier, Rabbi Elazar had answered Reish Lakish's objection about a man's priestly status with a particular retort. Later, with Rabbi Yohanan present, a similar case arose and Reish Lakish raised the same objection, and Rabbi Yohanan gave the very same retort. Reish Lakish realized Rabbi Elazar had been quoting Yohanan and angrily scolded him for not saying so.

08.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Yosei
08.event: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a woman may perform halitza within three months of her husband's death, was told no, and objected.
08.turn: Rabbi Yosei answered the objection by citing a verse showing that only one eligible for levirate marriage is eligible for halitza.
08.outcome: The ruling stands: no halitza within three months.
08.summary: A man came to Rabbi Yosei and asked whether halitza could be done within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said no, and when the man asked what harm there would be, Rabbi Yosei recited a verse proving that halitza applies only to a woman who could enter levirate marriage.
08.missing: The exchange is a halakhic Q and A with only a thin scene and no personal turn or consequence; the man's reaction is not given.

09.missing: A baraita deriving the dates of Moses' death and birth from verses; it cites biblical events only as proof texts, not as a story told.

10.event: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda forbade Meir's students from entering his study house, but Sumakhos pushed in and taught a ruling from Meir.
10.turn: Rabbi Yehuda grew angry at his own students and dismissed the ruling as irrelevant, so Rabbi Yosei warned that people would say Meir died, Yehuda got angry and Yosei stayed silent.
10.outcome: Rabbi Yosei broke his silence and argued the ruling was relevant after all.
10.summary: Rabbi Yehuda barred Rabbi Meir's students, calling them troublemakers, but Sumakhos forced his way in and recited a ruling of Meir. Rabbi Yehuda became angry and said the case was impossible since a woman would not be in the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Yosei, who had been silent, declared that he would not let it be said the Torah suffered through his silence, and argued that the case was indeed relevant.
10.missing: The dispute is left to the later discussion; the story ends with Yosei's argument.

11.actor: A man selling glass beads and a woman customer
11.event: A woman asked a man selling glass beads for one string, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it.
11.turn: She replied 'Give, give,' which Rav Hama interpreted as mockery rather than agreement.
11.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that such repeated 'give, give' means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
11.summary: A man was selling glass beads when a woman asked him for one string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she answered 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that this meant nothing, as she was only mocking him, so no betrothal took place.

12.missing: A single clause (they offered the omer and then ate) is part of a legal argument about the new crop, not a narrative.

13.actor: Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai, Reish Lakish, Rabba bar bar Hanna
13.event: Three sages each report personally seeing the land flowing with milk and honey; Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai once rose early and walked ankle-deep in fig honey between Lud and Ono.
13.summary: Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai says that one morning he walked ankle-deep in honey from figs between Lud and Ono. Reish Lakish and Rabba bar bar Hanna then each say they saw regions flowing with milk and honey of stated sizes.
13.missing: These are eyewitness testimonies about the land's abundance; there is no turn or outcome beyond the sightings.

14.missing: Rabbi Yohanan's recollections of studying with Rabbi Oshaya are statements and a Gemara challenge about them, not an event with a turn.

15.actor: Rabbi Hanina, his wife, and a pauper
15.event: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent four dinars every Shabbat eve to a pauper, and one day sent them with his wife.
15.turn: She came back saying he did not need it, having overheard him being asked whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
15.outcome: Rabbi Hanina answered by quoting Rabbi Elazar that we should appreciate swindlers, since without them we would sin by neglecting the truly poor.
15.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send a pauper four dinars each Shabbat eve, and once sent them with his wife. She returned and said the man needed nothing, as she heard people inside asking whether he ate off silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina said we should be grateful to swindlers, because they give us an excuse for any failure to help the truly poor.

16.actor: Manasseh, king of Israel, and the prophet Isaiah
16.event: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai found a lineage scroll in Jerusalem saying Manasseh killed Isaiah; Rava then tells how Manasseh put Isaiah on trial.
16.turn: Manasseh confronted Isaiah with his prophecies that contradicted Moses; Isaiah, knowing he would not be believed, uttered a divine name and was swallowed in a cedar.
16.outcome: Manasseh's men sawed the cedar in two, and Isaiah died when the saw reached his mouth, punished for calling the people unclean of lips.
16.summary: A scroll found by Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai recorded that Manasseh killed Isaiah. Manasseh judged Isaiah, accusing him of contradicting Moses, and Isaiah, sure he would not be heard, vanished into a cedar by uttering a divine name. Manasseh had the tree sawed in two, and Isaiah died when the saw reached his mouth.
16.missing: The passage itself holds only the scroll claim; the story is told in the context segments that follow.

17.actor: A man claiming to be from Shot Mishot and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
17.event: A man told the Sages he was from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood up and said it lies between the rivers.
17.outcome: The exchange moves to a legal question about lineage status of the area between the rivers.
17.summary: A man told the Sages that he came from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stood and declared that the place lies between the rivers. The Gemara then explains what that means for lineage law.
17.missing: No clear outcome for the man; the incident only sets up a geographic and legal discussion.

18.event: On going up to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Zeira found no ferry and crossed the Jordan by holding a rope.
18.turn: A Sadducee mocked him as hasty, like those who said 'we will do' before 'we will hear'.
18.outcome: Rabbi Zeira replied that Moses and Aaron did not merit this place, so he could not be sure he would, and hurried across.
18.summary: Rabbi Zeira could not find a ferry across the Jordan on his way to Eretz Yisrael, so he crossed holding a rope. A Sadducee taunted him for still being hasty. Rabbi Zeira answered that Moses and Aaron never merited to enter, so he could not be sure he would, and did not want to risk waiting.

19.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
19.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with a rough cloth thrown over his head, hurrying his child to the synagogue.
19.turn: Asked why the fuss, Yehoshua ben Levi pointed to the verse linking teaching one's children with standing at Sinai.
19.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never again ate before teaching a child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna took up the same practice.
19.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue with a scrap of cloth on his head and asked what the rush was about. Yehoshua ben Levi answered that the Torah ties teaching children to the day Israel stood at Sinai. From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not taste breakfast until he had taught a child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna did likewise.

20.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef, Rav Shmuel, and Rabba
20.event: Mar Yehuda met Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at Rabba's study hall door and posed a contradiction between two baraitot.
20.turn: They were silent and could not answer, so they brought it before Rabba.
20.outcome: Rabba said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved it by saying the first baraita dealt with an animal found to be a tereifa.
20.summary: Mar Yehuda found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at Rabba's study hall and cited a baraita, then raised a contradicting one. They had no answer, so they took the difficulty to Rabba, who joked that a troublemaker had put them up to it and resolved the contradiction with a distinction.
20.missing: This is a scholastic exchange with a thin scene; the people matter only as carriers of a legal question.
